title: We did it ourselves
hookLine: the best leaders are barely noticed, and people say "we did it ourselves" (Tao Te Ching 17)
last: RETURNING TO THE ROOT IS STILLNESS.

lines: A HAND ON THE BACK OF THE SEAT.
cards: A kid is learning to ride a bike. A parent runs alongside, one hand on the back of the seat, steadying it. Then, without saying anything, the parent lets go.

The kid keeps pedaling, wobbles, steadies, and rides to the end of the street alone, then turns around, beaming: I did it! And the parent, out of breath, says: you did. Not a word about the hand on the seat.
Chapter seventeen of the Tao Te Ching says that moment is what the best kind of leading looks like.

teach.b: First, a ladder of leaders. With the best, the chapter says, people barely know they're there. Next, people love and praise them.
Next, people fear them. And at the bottom, people mock them. Love and praise land second, not first: a leader everyone praises is still standing in the center of the picture.
The best one has stepped out of it. Second, trust.

teach.h: NOT ENOUGH TRUST, NO TRUST BACK.
teach.b: A short, sharp line: where there isn't enough trust, there will be no trust in return. A leader who doesn't trust people breeds people who don't trust the leader.
The best leader steps back partly because they trust the people to do the work. Third, the quiet hand.
The best leaders are unhurried and careful with their words. They do what's needed, without speeches, and go quiet again. Fourth, the ending that names today's lesson.
When the work is done and things turn out well, the people all say: this happened by itself; we did it ourselves.
The word underneath is ziran: of itself so, or natural. The chapter counts it as success when nobody gives the leader the credit. That can be hard to want.

But a parent, a teacher, a manager, a friend, anyone who has helped someone grow, has had the chance to be that hand on the seat: steadying, then letting go, and letting the joy belong to someone else.

how: Some teachers, parents and managers who read the Tao Te Ching take chapter seventeen as a model: they help quietly and step back, so the people they help can own the result.

games.q: what does “we did it ourselves” mean?
o: a team's cheer after beating a stronger rival
what people say when the best leader goes unnoticed
a boast that nobody ever needs any help

games.q: chapter seventeen's ladder: tap the pairs.

s: chapter seventeen puts the leaders people love and praise at the top
they're second. the best are barely noticed.
the chapter says where trust is lacking, there will be no trust in return
a leader who doesn't trust breeds people who don't trust back.
at the end, the people thank their leader
they say it happened by itself: we did it ourselves.

games.q: you quietly helped a friend fix a problem. now they're telling everyone, "I figured it out myself." what do you do?
o: remind them, kindly, that you helped.
let them say it, and be glad.
tell the others what really happened.
games.why: in chapter seventeen, success is when the work is done and the people say, we did it ourselves.

practice: Bring to mind someone you could help, a coworker stuck on something, a kid with homework, a friend making a decision, and picture helping in a way that leaves them holding the result: a question instead of an answer, a hand on the seat, then letting go.
Notice whether part of you wants them to know it was you; that's all right, so just notice it and let it rest.

wordCard.voice: We did it ourselves. Chapter seventeen's sign of the best leading: the work gets done, and the people say it happened of itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: of itself so, natural. What the people say in chapter seventeen's last line.

carryVoice: Your line: they did it themselves. The joy of the ride belongs to the rider. See you tomorrow.
